title: Quality of healthcare information on YouTube: psoriatic arthritis
screen_reason: Content analysis of the first 200 YouTube videos for 'psoriatic arthritis' (155 after exclusions). Two rheumatologists classified each video as useful (completely scientifically accurate) or misleading (containing any inaccurate information) against ACR/EULAR guidelines: 23/155 (14.8%) were misleading - a CONTENT falsity share against an external ground truth with an explicit denominator.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language YouTube search in incognito mode; authors based in Turkey)
estimates.date: Search performed 18 April 2021; videos uploaded 30 March 2011 to 26 March 2021
estimates.measure_type: % of YouTube videos on psoriatic arthritis containing misleading (inaccurate) information
estimates.denominator: 155 videos analysed, from the first 200 YouTube results for the keyword 'psoriatic arthritis' (relevance mode, incognito), after excluding 1 duplicate, 17 irrelevant, 7 non-English, 4 longer than one hour, 10 music videos and 6 advertisements
estimates.definition: Video classified 'misleading' if it contained ANY inaccurate information regarding any aspect of psoriatic arthritis, judged against the guidelines of professional rheumatology organizations (ACR, EULAR); 'useful' required the information to be completely scientifically accurate
estimates.misinfo_def: 'The videos were deemed useful if the information they contained was completely scientifically accurate, and misleading if they contained any inaccurate information regarding any aspect of PsA, in accordance with the guidelines of professional organizations in the field of rheumatology such as the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR).'
estimates.source_quote: A total of 132 (85.2%) videos revealed useful information about PsA, whereas the remaining 23 (14.8%) were misleading.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (the quoted span); the same figure in Results, 'Assessment of usefulness', p. S33, and Table 3
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two rheumatologists (MEO, OZ) blindly analysed each video, discrepancies resolved by re-evaluation and consensus; accuracy judged against ACR/EULAR professional guidelines. Cohen's kappa is reported for the instrument scores (0.783 modified DISCERN, 0.862 JAMA, 0.824 GQS) but NOT for the useful/misleading classification itself.
estimates.moderator_quote: A YouTube search was performed on April 18, 2021, using the keyword “psoriatic arthritis.” The “incognito” mode of Google Chrome ... was used for browsing YouTube. Browsing history was deleted prior to the search to prevent results from being influenced by previous online activity. YouTube's default relevance mode was used to mimic most consumers' search pattern ... therefore, the first 200 videos regarding PsA were listed
estimates.notes: source_quote is the Abstract sentence; the Results state the same figure as 'Of the total 155 videos evaluated, 132 (85.2%) were categorized as useful, while 23 (14.8%) contained misleading information.', which the three-column text rendering splits across interleaved columns and hyphenates, so it cannot be quoted as one contiguous span. CONTENT rather than QUALITY even though the paper's title says 'quality': the useful/misleading dichotomy is an accuracy judgement against clinical guidelines, and a wholly accurate video cannot be labelled misleading (the trigger is 'any inaccurate information'), which is the test §3 sets. The separate GQS/JAMA/modified DISCERN instruments ARE quality scores but are reported only as medians (mDISCERN 3, JAMA 3, GQS 4), so per the instructions they yield no rows. breadth coded 'false' because the criterion is factual inaccuracy, though the paper's label for it is 'misleading'. Rank-truncated frame (first 200 results) hence denom_selection=curated.

estimates.measure_type: % of the 10 most-viewed psoriatic arthritis videos containing misleading information

estimates.denominator: the 10 highest-viewed ('high-performer') videos among the 155 analysed
estimates.definition: Video classified 'misleading' (containing any inaccurate information about PsA, against ACR/EULAR guidelines)

estimates.source_quote: ing, and detected one misleading video
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two rheumatologist raters and the same guideline-based accuracy criterion.
estimates.moderator_quote: In addition, we compared the top 10 high-performer videos with the remaining 145 videos and detected no significant difference concerning the number of useful and misleading videos between the two groups (p = 0.546)
estimates.notes: The full sentence is 'We also conducted an extra analysis to assess how the top 10 high-performer videos (in regard to the number of views) were separated into useful and misleading, and detected one misleading video (10%).' In the three-column text rendering it is broken into one-line fragments interleaved with the other columns, so no contiguous span holds both the count and the percentage: source_quote carries the numerator fragment (starting mid-word after the hyphenated 'mislead-|ing'), and the next fragment reads verbatim '(10%). In addition, we compared the top'. Most-viewed subset of the same corpus (1/10 videos), reported by the authors as a separate analysis; kept because a view-ranked estimate is a distinct methodological variant, but n=10 makes it extremely imprecise and the authors found no significant difference from the remaining 145 videos. An adjudicator may reasonably drop this row on precision grounds.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted (source/content subgroups, not the paper's headline): independent users posted the highest share of misleading videos, 6/10 = 60% ('Independent users constituted the source that posted the highest percentage of misleading videos (6/10, 60%)'; Table 3 gives independent users 4 useful / 6 misleading); all videos from universities and professional organizations were useful (0/20 misleading); physicians 3/42, health information websites 11/71, TV programmes 3/12 misleading (computable from Table 3's column percentages but reported only as shares of the misleading column, i.e. 13%, 47.8%, 13% of the 23 misleading videos, which are within-misinformation composition figures); 5/19 (26.3%) of videos about patients' personal experience were misleading; 'all of the misleading videos were aimed at patients' (23/23, 100%). Not extracted (quality instruments reported as medians only, no share above a threshold): modified DISCERN 3, JAMA 3, GQS 4 overall, and their useful-vs-misleading contrasts. Not extracted (cited from other studies, excluded by R8): 63% psoriasis (Mueller et al.), 33% hypertension (Kumar et al.), 26% Ebola (Pathak et al.), 30% rheumatoid arthritis (Singh et al.), 16% SLE, 14% spondyloarthritis. Also noted: the video-source distribution of the whole corpus (health information websites 45.8%, physicians 27.1%, universities/professional organizations 12.9%, TV 7.7%, independent users 6.4%) and the 1.15% interaction rate - neither is a veracity share.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. Frame: the first 200 videos returned for 'psoriatic arthritis' on 18 April 2021, searched in Chrome incognito with browsing history cleared, YouTube default relevance sort; 155 retained after excluding 1 duplicate, 17 irrelevant, 7 non-English, 4 over one hour, 10 music videos, 6 advertisements. Rank-truncated convenience frame, single search day, English only, no geographic control. Two rheumatologists rated every video blindly, with discrepancies resolved by re-evaluation and consensus; Cohen's kappa reported for the instruments (mDISCERN 0.783, JAMA 0.862, GQS 0.824) but NOT for the useful/misleading judgement that produces the prevalence estimate. Accuracy criterion anchored to ACR/EULAR guidelines. Denominators are explicit throughout (Table 3), and the useful/misleading split is reported with counts.
